elements.evidence: The added operative language permits Customer to terminate “this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience.”

elements.element: Customer’s convenience termination requires 30 days’ prior notice.
elements.evidence: The clause requires “thirty days’ prior” notice.

elements.element: Customer’s convenience-termination notice must be written.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly requires “written notice to Vendor.”

elements.element: Vendor must refund prepaid fees following Customer’s convenience termination.
elements.evidence: The clause states that “Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees.”

elements.element: The refund must be calculated pro rata for the period after the effective date of termination.
elements.evidence: The refund covers prepaid Fees “pro rata for the period after the effective date of termination.”

elements.element: Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly states that “Vendor has no right to terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience during a committed term.”
Customer may terminate the Agreement or any Order Form for convenience.

elements.element: Customer’s convenience-termination notice period must be between 60 and 90 days.
elements.evidence: The operative notice period is 30 days, outside the required 60–90-day range.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee charged to Customer must not exceed three months’ fees.
elements.evidence: No early-termination fee is imposed, so the conditional cap is not triggered and no fee exceeds three months’ fees.
The clause does not affirmatively grant Vendor a convenience-termination right; it instead denies such a right during a committed term.

elements.element: Any Vendor termination for convenience may take effect only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Vendor is expressly denied a convenience-termination right during a committed term, thereby preventing an in-term convenience termination.

elements.element: If Vendor may terminate for convenience, Vendor must provide 90 days’ notice.
elements.evidence: No Vendor convenience-termination right is granted, so the condition triggering the 90-day notice requirement is demonstrably absent.

result.reason: The operative addition fully implements the preferred position: Customer receives a 30-day written convenience-termination right, prepaid Fees are refunded pro rata for the post-termination period, and Vendor has no corresponding right during a committed term. It does not independently satisfy the fallback because the Customer notice period is not within 60–90 days and Vendor is not affirmatively granted an end-of-term convenience-termination right. The change is targeted and leaves the existing term, expiration, breach, insolvency, and cause-based termination provisions effective.
